    print("  and then e(.,0) is constant.  The model is inhabited only by the")
    print("  trivial group -- every theorem proved in it would be vacuous.")

    rule("8. BLS in the corrected asymmetric setting over (Z/7)^2")
    S = BLSSetting(7)
    print(f"  g1 = {S.g1},  g2 = {S.g2},  order of zeta = e(g1,g2) is {S.root_order()}")
    sk, h = 4, 5
    pk, hp = S.public_key(sk), S.hash_point(h)
    sig = S.sign(sk, h)
    print(f"  sk = {sk}, message hash exponent h = {h}")
    print(f"  pk = {pk},  H = {hp},  signature = {sig}")
    print(f"  e(sigma, g2) = {S.e(sig, S.g2)}   e(H, pk) = {S.e(hp, pk)}")
    report("honest signature verifies", S.verifies(pk, hp, sig))
    report("correctness for all 49 key/message pairs", check_bls_correctness(7))
    report("exact criterion s = sk*h (mod 7) over all 343 triples => uniqueness",
           check_verification_criterion(7))
    print("  Accepted candidates s*g1 for (sk,h) = (4,5):",
          [s for s in range(7) if S.verifies(pk, hp, smul(7, s, S.g1))],
          f" (sk*h mod 7 = {(sk * h) % 7})")

    rule("9. Aggregation over (Z/5)^2 with 3 signers")
    report("aggregate correctness (all key/message tuples)",
           check_aggregate_correctness(5, 3))
    report("aggregate-to-single forgery extraction", check_forgery_extraction(5, 3))
    report("the extracted forgery IS the CDH target", check_cdh_reduction(5, 3))
    report("batch verification sound and complete (2 signers over (Z/3)^2)",
           check_batch_verification(3, 2))

    S5 = BLSSetting(5)
    sks, hs = (2, 3, 4), (1, 1, 1)
    pks = [S5.public_key(k) for k in sks]
    hpts = [S5.hash_point(x) for x in hs]
    sigs = [S5.sign(k, x) for k, x in zip(sks, hs)]
    agg = S5.aggregate(sigs)
    print(f"  individual signatures : {sigs}")
    print(f"  aggregate             : {agg}   (one group element, not three)")
    report("aggregate verifies", S5.agg_verifies(pks, hpts, agg))

    rule("10. Exact compression:  N^m signature tuples  -->  N aggregates")
    for n, m in ((3, 2), (3, 3), (5, 2)):
        total, image, N = compression_profile(n, m)
        print(f"  n = {n}, m = {m}:  tuples = N^m = {total:6d}   "
              f"distinct aggregates = {image:3d}   N = {N}")
        report(f"image is the whole group (compression {total} ->> {N})", image == N)

    rule("11. The rogue-key attack: registration is necessary")
    Sr = BLSSetting(5)
    pk1 = Sr.public_key(3)          # honest victim, secret key 3
    y = 4                            # adversary's chosen scalar
    pk2 = Sr.rogue_public_key(y, pk1)
    hpt = (2, 1)                     # any common message hash
    forged = smul(5, y, hpt)
    print(f"  victim public key pk1 = {pk1}")
    print(f"  rogue key pk2 = y*g2 - pk1 = {pk2}   (no secret key known)")
    print(f"  forged aggregate sigma = y*H = {forged}")
    report("the forged two-signer aggregate VERIFIES",
           Sr.agg_verifies([pk1, pk2], [hpt, hpt], forged))
    report("the attack succeeds for every y, victim key and message over (Z/5)^2",
           check_rogue_key_attack(5))
    print("  Hence aggregate security genuinely requires registered keys /")
    print("  proofs of possession: without them the scheme is broken outright.")

    print("\nAll demonstrations complete.\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: End-to-End Exhaustive Verification of the Pairing and Signature Theory
demos.description: A single self-contained program that reproduces every result of the development by exhaustive enumeration inside the determinant model (Z/n)², never by sampling. It checks alternation, skew-symmetry, bi-additivity and Z-bilinearity over all 625 pairs of (Z/5)²; the forcing theorem e(a·e₁+b·e₂, c·e₁+d·e₂) = ζ^(ad−bc) over all pairings and all coefficient tuples for n = 4 and n = 5; the classification, confirming for n = 5, 6, 8, 9, 12 that the nondegenerate scalars are exactly the units and that their count is φ(n); the rank obstruction, that the pairing vanishes identically on every cyclic subgroup; the endomorphism determinant law over all 81 matrices on (Z/3)² and the degree law e(mv,mw) = e(v,w)^(m²); the MOV table showing a ↦ e(aP,Q) is injective; the collapse of decisional Diffie–Hellman, verifying over all 343 triples that the publicly computable pairing test matches the hidden relation c ≡ ab exactly; the impossibility of the symmetric model, by searching all generators G for injectivity of P ↦ e(P,G) and finding none; BLS correctness over all 49 key/message pairs and the exact verification criterion s ≡ sk·h (mod 7) over all 343 triples, which is signature uniqueness in tabular form; aggregate correctness, aggregate-to-single forgery extraction and the identification of the extracted forgery with the Diffie–Hellman target for three signers over (Z/5)²; soundness and completeness of weighted batch verification; the exact compression counts N^m ↠ N; and finally the rogue-key attack, confirmed to succeed for every choice of adversarial scalar, victim key and message.
demos.code:
"""
Alternating pairings, the determinant form, and aggregate BLS signatures
========================================================================

Self-contained numerical demonstration of every result in the accompanying
paper, carried out inside the *determinant model*:

    A      = (Z/n) x (Z/n)                 the "torsion group"
    mu_n   = Z/n written multiplicatively  the target group of n-th roots of unity
    e(v,w) = zeta_0 ^ det(v,w),  det(v,w) = v1*w2 - v2*w1   (mod n)

We represent an element zeta_0^k of mu_n by its exponent k in Z/n, so that the
multiplicative group law of mu_n is addition mod n.  Every identity of the
paper is then a statement about integers mod n, and can be checked by
exhaustive enumeration over the whole parameter space.

Contents
--------
 1. The determinant pairing and its basic laws (skew-symmetry, bilinearity,
    blindness on cyclic subgroups).
 2. The forcing theorem: bi-additivity + alternation => determinant form.
 3. Classification: every alternating pairing is u*det; nondegenerate iff u is
    a unit.  Counting nondegenerate pairings = phi(n).
 4. Rank obstruction: on a cyclic subgroup the pairing is identically trivial.
 5. Endomorphism/degree law: e(Mv, Mw) = e(v,w)^det(M);  e(mv,mw)=e(v,w)^(m^2).
 6. MOV embedding and the collapse of decisional Diffie-Hellman.
 7. The obstruction theorem for the symmetric model with injective
    P |-> e(P,G): it forces the whole group to be trivial.
 8. BLS in the corrected asymmetric setting: correctness, the exact
    verification criterion s = sk*h (mod n), uniqueness.
 9. Aggregation: correctness, uniqueness, aggregate-to-single extraction,
    the CDH reduction, batch verification.
10. Exact compression:  N^m signatures  -->  N aggregates.
11. The rogue-key attack.

Run with:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from math import gcd
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vec = Tuple[int, int]  # element of (Z/n)^2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The determinant pairing
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def elements(n: int) -> List[Vec]:
    """All elements of the group (Z/n)^2."""
    return [(a, b) for a in range(n) for b in range(n)]


def add(n: int, v: Vec, w: Vec) -> Vec:
    """Group addition in (Z/n)^2."""
    return ((v[0] + w[0]) % n, (v[1] + w[1]) % n)


def sub(n: int, v: Vec, w: Vec) -> Vec:
    """Group subtraction in (Z/n)^2."""
    return ((v[0] - w[0]) % n, (v[1] - w[1]) % n)


def smul(n: int, k: int, v: Vec) -> Vec:
    """Scalar action of k in Z on (Z/n)^2."""
    return ((k * v[0]) % n, (k * v[1]) % n)


def det_form(n: int, v: Vec, w: Vec) -> int:
    """The determinant form det(v,w) = v1*w2 - v2*w1 in Z/n."""
    return (v[0] * w[1] - v[1] * w[0]) % n


def pairing(n: int, u: int) -> Callable[[Vec, Vec], int]:
    """
    The alternating pairing with scalar u:  e_u(v,w) = zeta_0^(u * det(v,w)).
    Returned as the exponent map (v,w) |-> u*det(v,w) mod n, since the target
    group mu_n is represented additively by its exponents.
    """
    def e(v: Vec, w: Vec) -> int:
        return (u * det_form(n, v, w)) % n
    return e


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2-3. Basic laws, forcing, classification
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def check_basic_laws(n: int) -> Dict[str, bool]:
    """Alternation, skew-symmetry, bi-additivity, Z-bilinearity."""
    e = pairing(n, 1)
    els = elements(n)
    alternating = all(e(v, v) == 0 for v in els)
    skew = all((e(v, w) + e(w, v)) % n == 0 for v in els for w in els)
    biadd_left = all(
        e(add(n, v, w), z) == (e(v, z) + e(w, z)) % n
        for v in els for w in els for z in els
    )
    biadd_right = all(
        e(v, add(n, w, z)) == (e(v, w) + e(v, z)) % n
        for v in els for w in els for z in els
    )
    bilinear = all(
        e(smul(n, k, v), w) == (k * e(v, w)) % n
        for k in range(n) for v in els for w in els
    )
    return {
        "alternating e(v,v)=1": alternating,
        "skew-symmetry e(w,v)=e(v,w)^-1": skew,
        "additive in first slot": biadd_left,
        "additive in second slot": biadd_right,
        "Z-bilinear e(kv,w)=e(v,w)^k": bilinear,
    }


def check_forcing_theorem(n: int) -> bool:
    """
    Forcing theorem:  e(a*eps1 + b*eps2, c*eps1 + d*eps2) = zeta^(ad-bc)
    where zeta = e(eps1, eps2).  Checked for every alternating pairing
    (i.e. every scalar u) and all integer coefficients mod n.
    """
    eps1, eps2 = (1, 0), (0, 1)
    for u in range(n):
        e = pairing(n, u)
        zeta = e(eps1, eps2)  # exponent of the root of unity
        for a, b, c, d in product(range(n), repeat=4):
            left = e(
                add(n, smul(n, a, eps1), smul(n, b, eps2)),
                add(n, smul(n, c, eps1), smul(n, d, eps2)),
            )
            right = (zeta * (a * d - b * c)) % n
            if left != right:
                return False
    return True


def is_nondegenerate(n: int, e: Callable[[Vec, Vec], int]) -> bool:
    """No nonzero v pairs trivially with everything."""
    for v in elements(n):
        if v == (0, 0):
            continue
        if all(e(v, w) == 0 for w in elements(n)):
            return False
    return True


def euler_phi(n: int) -> int:
    """Euler's totient, by direct counting."""
    return sum(1 for a in range(n) if gcd(a, n) == 1)


def classify_pairings(n: int) -> Tuple[List[int], int]:
    """
    Return the list of scalars u for which e_u is nondegenerate, together with
    phi(n).  Theorem: these coincide with the units of Z/n.
    """
    nondeg = [u for u in range(n) if is_nondegenerate(n, pairing(n, u))]
    return nondeg, euler_phi(n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4-5. Rank obstruction, degree law, endomorphisms
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def check_cyclic_blindness(n: int) -> bool:
    """e(a*v, b*v) = 1 for all a,b and all v: an alternating pairing sees
    nothing inside a cyclic subgroup.  This is the rank obstruction."""
    e = pairing(n, 1)
    return all(
        e(smul(n, a, v), smul(n, b, v)) == 0
        for a in range(n) for b in range(n) for v in elements(n)
    )


def lin_map(n: int, m: Tuple[int, int, int, int], v: Vec) -> Vec:
    """Apply the endomorphism with matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] to v."""
    a, b, c, d = m
    return ((a * v[0] + b * v[1]) % n, (c * v[0] + d * v[1]) % n)


def check_endomorphism_law(n: int) -> bool:
    """det(Mv, Mw) = det(M) * det(v,w) for every 2x2 matrix over Z/n."""
    for m in product(range(n), repeat=4):
        a, b, c, d = m
        dm = (a * d - b * c) % n
        for v, w in product(elements(n), repeat=2):
            if det_form(n, lin_map(n, m, v), lin_map(n, m, w)) != (dm * det_form(n, v, w)) % n:
                return False
    return True


def check_degree_law(n: int) -> bool:
    """e(mv, mw) = e(v,w)^(m^2): the scalar matrix case of the endomorphism law."""
    e = pairing(n, 1)
    return all(
        e(smul(n, m, v), smul(n, m, w)) == (m * m * e(v, w)) % n
        for m in range(n) for v, w in product(elements(n), repeat=2)
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. MOV embedding and DDH
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def mov_table(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """
    With P = eps1, Q = eps2 and zeta = e(P,Q) of exact order n, the map
    a |-> e(aP, Q) = zeta^a is injective on {0,...,n-1}: the curve discrete
    logarithm embeds into the discrete logarithm in mu_n.
    """
    e = pairing(n, 1)
    p, q = (1, 0), (0, 1)
    return [e(smul(n, a, p), q) for a in range(n)]


def ddh_test(n: int, a: int, b: int, c: int) -> bool:
    """
    The publicly computable DDH distinguisher:  e(aP, bQ) =? e(P, cQ).
    Inputs are only the *group elements* aP, bQ, cQ -- never a, b, c.
    """
    e = pairing(n, 1)
    p, q = (1, 0), (0, 1)
    aP, bQ, cQ = smul(n, a, p), smul(n, b, q), smul(n, c, q)
    return e(aP, bQ) == e(p, cQ)


def check_ddh_collapse(n: int) -> bool:
    """The test succeeds exactly when c = ab mod n: DDH is easy."""
    return all(
        ddh_test(n, a, b, c) == ((a * b) % n == c % n)
        for a, b, c in product(range(n), repeat=3)
    )


def check_ddh_blind_on_cyclic(n: int) -> bool:
    """On a single cyclic subgroup the same test is vacuous: both sides are 1."""
    e = pairing(n, 1)
    p = (1, 0)
    return all(
        e(smul(n, a, p), smul(n, b, p)) == 0 and e(p, smul(n, c, p)) == 0
        for a, b, c in product(range(n), repeat=3)
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. The obstruction theorem for the symmetric model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def symmetric_model_injective_generators(n: int) -> List[Vec]:
    """
    Search for a generator G such that P |-> e(P, G) is injective on the whole
    group.  The obstruction theorem says: none exists unless the group is
    trivial (n = 1).  Alternation gives e(G,G) = 1 = e(0,G), forcing G = 0,
    and then e(.,0) is constant.
    """
    e = pairing(n, 1)
    els = elements(n)
    good: List[Vec] = []
    for g in els:
        images = [e(pt, g) for pt in els]
        if len(set(images)) == len(els):
            good.append(g)
    return good


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. BLS in the corrected asymmetric setting
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

class BLSSetting:
    """
    The corrected (type-3) BLS setting over the determinant model:

        g1 = (1,0)  signature generator,   g2 = (0,1)  key generator,
        zeta = e(g1, g2) has exact order n.

    public key  pk(sk) = sk * g2
    hash point  H(h)   = h  * g1
    signature   sig    = (sk*h) * g1
    verify      e(sigma, g2) == e(H, pk)
    """

    def __init__(self, n: int) -> None:
        self.n = n
        self.g1: Vec = (1, 0)
        self.g2: Vec = (0, 1)
        self.e = pairing(n, 1)

    # --- scheme --------------------------------------------------------
    def public_key(self, sk: int) -> Vec:
        return smul(self.n, sk, self.g2)

    def hash_point(self, h: int) -> Vec:
        return smul(self.n, h, self.g1)

    def sign(self, sk: int, h: int) -> Vec:
        return smul(self.n, sk * h, self.g1)

    def verifies(self, pk: Vec, hpt: Vec, sigma: Vec) -> bool:
        return self.e(sigma, self.g2) == self.e(hpt, pk)

    # --- root of unity -------------------------------------------------
    def root_order(self) -> int:
        """Exact order of zeta = e(g1, g2) in mu_n."""
        zeta = self.e(self.g1, self.g2)
        k = 1
        while (k * zeta) % self.n != 0:
            k += 1
        return k

    # --- aggregation ---------------------------------------------------
    def aggregate(self, sigmas: Sequence[Vec]) -> Vec:
        out: Vec = (0, 0)
        for s in sigmas:
            out = add(self.n, out, s)
        return out

    def agg_verifies(self, pks: Sequence[Vec], hpts: Sequence[Vec], sigma: Vec) -> bool:
        """e(sigma, g2) == prod_i e(H_i, pk_i); the product is a sum of exponents."""
        rhs = 0
        for pk, hpt in zip(pks, hpts):
            rhs = (rhs + self.e(hpt, pk)) % self.n
        return self.e(sigma, self.g2) == rhs

    def batch_verifies(
        self,
        pks: Sequence[Vec],
        hpts: Sequence[Vec],
        sigs: Sequence[Vec],
        weights: Sequence[int],
    ) -> bool:
        lhs_pt: Vec = (0, 0)
        for r, s in zip(weights, sigs):
            lhs_pt = add(self.n, lhs_pt, smul(self.n, r, s))
        rhs = 0
        for r, pk, hpt in zip(weights, pks, hpts):
            rhs = (rhs + r * self.e(hpt, pk)) % self.n
        return self.e(lhs_pt, self.g2) == rhs

    # --- rogue key -----------------------------------------------------
    def rogue_public_key(self, y: int, pk1: Vec) -> Vec:
        """y*g2 - pk1: computable from the victim's public key alone."""
        return sub(self.n, smul(self.n, y, self.g2), pk1)


def check_bls_correctness(n: int) -> bool:
    """Every honest signature verifies (all n^2 key/message pairs)."""
    S = BLSSetting(n)
    return all(
        S.verifies(S.public_key(sk), S.hash_point(h), S.sign(sk, h))
        for sk in range(n) for h in range(n)
    )


def check_verification_criterion(n: int) -> bool:
    """
    Exact criterion: the candidate s*g1 is accepted  <=>  s = sk*h (mod n).
    Checked over all n^3 triples.  Equivalently, signatures are unique.
    """
    S = BLSSetting(n)
    for sk, h, s in product(range(n), repeat=3):
        accepted = S.verifies(S.public_key(sk), S.hash_point(h), smul(n, s, S.g1))
        if accepted != (s % n == (sk * h) % n):
            return False
    return True


def check_aggregate_correctness(n: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """The sum of m honest signatures satisfies the aggregate equation."""
    S = BLSSetting(n)
    for sks in product(range(n), repeat=m):
        for hs in product(range(n), repeat=m):
            pks = [S.public_key(sk) for sk in sks]
            hpts = [S.hash_point(h) for h in hs]
            sigma = S.aggregate([S.sign(sk, h) for sk, h in zip(sks, hs)])
            if not S.agg_verifies(pks, hpts, sigma):
                return False
    return True


def check_forgery_extraction(n: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """
    Aggregate-to-single extraction: from ANY sigma = t*g1 satisfying the
    aggregate equation, subtracting the known co-signer contributions yields a
    valid single-signer signature for the target index 0.
    """
    S = BLSSetting(n)
    for sks in product(range(n), repeat=m):
        for hs in product(range(n), repeat=m):
            pks = [S.public_key(sk) for sk in sks]
            hpts = [S.hash_point(h) for h in hs]
            for t in range(n):
                sigma = smul(n, t, S.g1)
                if not S.agg_verifies(pks, hpts, sigma):
                    continue
                cosigners = S.aggregate([S.sign(sks[i], hs[i]) for i in range(1, m)])
                extracted = sub(n, sigma, cosigners)
                if not S.verifies(pks[0], hpts[0], extracted):
                    return False
    return True


def check_cdh_reduction(n: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """
    The extracted forgery IS the computational Diffie-Hellman target
    T = a * H(h(m*)), where a = sk_0 is the challenge secret.
    """
    S = BLSSetting(n)
    for sks in product(range(n), repeat=m):
        for hs in product(range(n), repeat=m):
            pks = [S.public_key(sk) for sk in sks]
            hpts = [S.hash_point(h) for h in hs]
            target = smul(n, sks[0], hpts[0])  # CDH answer
            for t in range(n):
                sigma = smul(n, t, S.g1)
                if not S.agg_verifies(pks, hpts, sigma):
                    continue
                cosigners = S.aggregate([S.sign(sks[i], hs[i]) for i in range(1, m)])
                if sub(n, sigma, cosigners) != target:
                    return False
    return True


def check_batch_verification(n: int, m: int) -> bool:
    """
    A family passes every weighted batch check  <=>  every signature verifies
    individually.  The forward direction uses the indicator weights.
    """
    S = BLSSetting(n)
    all_weights = list(product(range(n), repeat=m))
    for sks in product(range(n), repeat=m):
        for hs in product(range(n), repeat=m):
            for ts in product(range(n), repeat=m):  # candidate signatures t_i*g1
                pks = [S.public_key(sk) for sk in sks]
                hpts = [S.hash_point(h) for h in hs]
                sigs = [smul(n, t, S.g1) for t in ts]
                all_batches = all(S.batch_verifies(pks, hpts, sigs, w) for w in all_weights)
                all_single = all(
                    S.verifies(pks[i], hpts[i], sigs[i]) for i in range(m)
                )
                if all_batches != all_single:
                    return False
    return True


def check_rogue_key_attack(n: int) -> bool:
    """
    Universal forgery without any secret key: with pk2 = y*g2 - pk1 and
    sigma = y*H, the two-signer aggregate equation holds for EVERY y, pk1, H.
    """
    S = BLSSetting(n)
    for y in range(n):
        for pk1 in elements(n):
            for hpt in elements(n):
                pk2 = S.rogue_public_key(y, pk1)
                sigma = smul(n, y, hpt)
                if not S.agg_verifies([pk1, pk2], [hpt, hpt], sigma):
                    return False
    return True


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 10. Exact compression
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def compression_profile(n: int, m: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """
    Return (N^m, |image of aggregation|, N).  Theorem: the image is all of the
    group, so aggregation realises exactly an N^m ->> N compression.
    """
    els = elements(n)
    N = len(els)
    image = set()
    for tup in product(els, repeat=m):
        acc: Vec = (0, 0)
        for v in tup:
            acc = add(n, acc, v)
        image.add(acc)
    return N ** m, len(image), N


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reporting
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def report(label: str, ok: bool) -> None:
    print(f"  [{'OK ' if ok else 'FAIL'}]  {label}")


def main() -> None:
    rule("1. Basic laws of the determinant pairing on (Z/5)^2")
    for label, ok in check_basic_laws(5).items():
        report(label, ok)

    rule("2. The forcing theorem: alternation + bi-additivity => determinant")
    report("e(a e1 + b e2, c e1 + d e2) = zeta^(ad-bc)  over (Z/4)^2, all pairings",
           check_forcing_theorem(4))
    report("same over (Z/5)^2", check_forcing_theorem(5))

    rule("3. Classification of alternating pairings e_u = u * det")
    for n in (5, 6, 8, 9, 12):
        nondeg, phi = classify_pairings(n)
        units = [u for u in range(n) if gcd(u, n) == 1]
        print(f"  n = {n:2d}:  nondegenerate scalars = {nondeg}")
        print(f"           units of Z/{n}          = {units}")
        report(f"nondegenerate  <=>  unit,  count = phi({n}) = {phi}",
               nondeg == units and len(nondeg) == phi)

    rule("4. Rank obstruction: the pairing is blind inside any cyclic subgroup")
    report("e(a v, b v) = 1 for all a, b, v over (Z/5)^2", check_cyclic_blindness(5))
    report("e(a v, b v) = 1 for all a, b, v over (Z/6)^2", check_cyclic_blindness(6))
    print("  Consequence: if the torsion were cyclic, nondegeneracy would force it")
    print("  to be trivial.  A nontrivial Weil pairing needs rank two.")

    rule("5. Endomorphism equivariance and the degree law")
    report("det(Mv, Mw) = det(M) det(v,w) over (Z/3)^2, all 81 matrices",
           check_endomorphism_law(3))
    report("e(mv, mw) = e(v,w)^(m^2) over (Z/5)^2", check_degree_law(5))

    rule("6. MOV embedding and the collapse of decisional Diffie-Hellman")
    n = 7
    tbl = mov_table(n)
    print(f"  a          : {list(range(n))}")
    print(f"  e(a P, Q)  : {tbl}   (exponents of zeta)")
    report("a |-> e(aP,Q) injective: curve DLP embeds into DLP in mu_n",
           len(set(tbl)) == n)
    report("DDH test e(aP,bQ) = e(P,cQ)  <=>  c = ab (mod 7)", check_ddh_collapse(7))
    report("the same test is vacuous on one cyclic subgroup",
           check_ddh_blind_on_cyclic(7))

    rule("7. Obstruction: the symmetric model with injective P |-> e(P,G)")
    for n in (2, 3, 5, 7):
        good = symmetric_model_injective_generators(n)
        report(f"n = {n}: no generator G makes P |-> e(P,G) injective", good == [])
    print("  Alternation gives e(G,G) = 1 = e(0,G), so injectivity forces G = 0,")
    print("  and then e(.,0) is constant.  The model is inhabited only by the")
    print("  trivial group -- every theorem proved in it would be vacuous.")

    rule("8. BLS in the corrected asymmetric setting over (Z/7)^2")
    S = BLSSetting(7)
    print(f"  g1 = {S.g1},  g2 = {S.g2},  order of zeta = e(g1,g2) is {S.root_order()}")
    sk, h = 4, 5
    pk, hp = S.public_key(sk), S.hash_point(h)
    sig = S.sign(sk, h)
    print(f"  sk = {sk}, message hash exponent h = {h}")
    print(f"  pk = {pk},  H = {hp},  signature = {sig}")
    print(f"  e(sigma, g2) = {S.e(sig, S.g2)}   e(H, pk) = {S.e(hp, pk)}")
    report("honest signature verifies", S.verifies(pk, hp, sig))
    report("correctness for all 49 key/message pairs", check_bls_correctness(7))
    report("exact criterion s = sk*h (mod 7) over all 343 triples => uniqueness",
           check_verification_criterion(7))
    print("  Accepted candidates s*g1 for (sk,h) = (4,5):",
          [s for s in range(7) if S.verifies(pk, hp, smul(7, s, S.g1))],
          f" (sk*h mod 7 = {(sk * h) % 7})")

    rule("9. Aggregation over (Z/5)^2 with 3 signers")
    report("aggregate correctness (all key/message tuples)",
           check_aggregate_correctness(5, 3))
    report("aggregate-to-single forgery extraction", check_forgery_extraction(5, 3))
    report("the extracted forgery IS the CDH target", check_cdh_reduction(5, 3))
    report("batch verification sound and complete (2 signers over (Z/3)^2)",
           check_batch_verification(3, 2))

    S5 = BLSSetting(5)
    sks, hs = (2, 3, 4), (1, 1, 1)
    pks = [S5.public_key(k) for k in sks]
    hpts = [S5.hash_point(x) for x in hs]
    sigs = [S5.sign(k, x) for k, x in zip(sks, hs)]
    agg = S5.aggregate(sigs)
    print(f"  individual signatures : {sigs}")
    print(f"  aggregate             : {agg}   (one group element, not three)")
    report("aggregate verifies", S5.agg_verifies(pks, hpts, agg))

    rule("10. Exact compression:  N^m signature tuples  -->  N aggregates")
    for n, m in ((3, 2), (3, 3), (5, 2)):
        total, image, N = compression_profile(n, m)
        print(f"  n = {n}, m = {m}:  tuples = N^m = {total:6d}   "
              f"distinct aggregates = {image:3d}   N = {N}")
        report(f"image is the whole group (compression {total} ->> {N})", image == N)

    rule("11. The rogue-key attack: registration is necessary")
    Sr = BLSSetting(5)
    pk1 = Sr.public_key(3)          # honest victim, secret key 3
    y = 4                            # adversary's chosen scalar
    pk2 = Sr.rogue_public_key(y, pk1)
    hpt = (2, 1)                     # any common message hash
    forged = smul(5, y, hpt)
    print(f"  victim public key pk1 = {pk1}")
    print(f"  rogue key pk2 = y*g2 - pk1 = {pk2}   (no secret key known)")
    print(f"  forged aggregate sigma = y*H = {forged}")
    report("the forged two-signer aggregate VERIFIES",
           Sr.agg_verifies([pk1, pk2], [hpt, hpt], forged))
    report("the attack succeeds for every y, victim key and message over (Z/5)^2",
           check_rogue_key_attack(5))
    print("  Hence aggregate security genuinely requires registered keys /")
    print("  proofs of possession: without them the scheme is broken outright.")

    print("\nAll demonstrations complete.\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Determinant-Model Pairing Evaluation and Nondegeneracy Certification
algorithms.description: Evaluates an arbitrary alternating pairing on (Z/n)² and issues a complete certificate of its structure. By the classification theorem every such pairing is e_u(v,w) = ζ^(u·det(v,w)) for a single scalar u, so the entire pairing is specified by u and evaluation is a single 2×2 determinant modulo n — O(1) arithmetic operations. The certificate reports whether the pairing is nondegenerate, the exact order n/gcd(u,n) of its root of unity, an explicit degeneracy witness (n/gcd(u,n), 0) when it is degenerate, and the automorphism scalar putting it into symplectic normal form when it is not. The decisive point is complexity: the naive nondegeneracy test enumerates all N² = n⁴ pairs, whereas the criterion 'nondegenerate ⟺ u is a unit' reduces the decision to a single gcd, i.e. O(log n). The routine also carries an O(n⁴) brute-force cross-check so the fast criterion can be audited against the definition.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: modulus n ≥ 1, scalar u ∈ Z/n
OUTPUT: certificate (nondegenerate?, ord ζ, degeneracy witness, normal-form automorphism)

1. EVALUATION
   function PAIR(v, w):
       return (u · (v₁·w₂ − v₂·w₁)) mod n        ▷ exponent of ζ; O(1)

2. FAST STRUCTURAL DECISION
   g ← gcd(u mod n, n)                            ▷ O(log n)
   nondegenerate ← (g = 1)
   ord ← n / g                                    ▷ exact order of ζ^u

3. WITNESS CONSTRUCTION (degenerate case)
   if g > 1:
       k ← n / g
       witness ← (k, 0)
       ▷ invariant: u·det((k,0), w) = u·k·w₂ ≡ 0 for every w, and (k,0) ≠ 0
   else:
       witness ← NONE

4. SYMPLECTIC NORMAL FORM (nondegenerate case)
   if g = 1:
       ψ ← multiplication by u                    ▷ automorphism of (Z/n)²
       ▷ invariant: e_u(v,w) = det(ψv, w) for all v, w

5. AUDIT (optional, O(n⁴))
   brute ← for every v ≠ 0, does some w give PAIR(v,w) ≠ 0 ?
   assert brute = nondegenerate

6. return (nondegenerate, ord, witness, ψ)
algorithms.code:
"""
Algorithm 1: Determinant-Model Weil Pairing Evaluation and
Nondegeneracy Certification.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from typing import Callable, List, Optional, Tuple

Vec = Tuple[int, int]


def det_form(n: int, v: Vec, w: Vec) -> int:
    """The alternating determinant form det(v,w) = v1*w2 - v2*w1 in Z/n."""
    return (v[0] * w[1] - v[1] * w[0]) % n


def pairing_exponent(n: int, u: int) -> Callable[[Vec, Vec], int]:
    """
    Return the alternating pairing with scalar u, represented by the exponent
    of the root of unity:  e_u(v, w) = zeta_0 ^ (u * det(v,w)).

    By the classification theorem every alternating pairing on (Z/n)^2 with
    values in mu_n arises this way for exactly one u in Z/n.
    """
    def e(v: Vec, w: Vec) -> int:
        return (u * det_form(n, v, w)) % n
    return e


def root_of_unity_order(n: int, u: int) -> int:
    """
    Exact order of zeta = e_u(eps1, eps2) inside mu_n.  Equals n / gcd(u, n),
    and by the nondegeneracy criterion equals n exactly when u is a unit.
    """
    return n // gcd(u % n, n)


def degeneracy_witness(n: int, u: int) -> Optional[Vec]:
    """
    Return a nonzero vector v that pairs trivially with everything, if one
    exists, else None.  Constructive form of the nondegeneracy criterion:
    with g = gcd(u, n) > 1 the vector (n/g, 0) is a witness.
    """
    g = gcd(u % n, n)
    if g == 1:
        return None
    k = n // g
    return (k % n, 0)


def is_nondegenerate(n: int, u: int) -> bool:
    """
    Decide nondegeneracy.  The naive test enumerates N^2 = n^4 pairs; the
    criterion below is O(log n) via a single gcd, and the two agree.
    """
    return gcd(u % n, n) == 1


def certify(n: int, u: int) -> dict:
    """
    Full certificate for the pairing e_u:
      * whether it is nondegenerate,
      * the exact order of its root of unity,
      * an explicit degeneracy witness when it is degenerate,
      * the automorphism scalar putting it in symplectic normal form
        (e_u(v,w) = det(psi v, w) with psi = multiplication by u), when
        nondegenerate.
    Complexity: O(log n).  The exhaustive cross-check is O(n^4).
    """
    nd = is_nondegenerate(n, u)
    return {
        "modulus": n,
        "scalar": u % n,
        "nondegenerate": nd,
        "root_order": root_of_unity_order(n, u),
        "degeneracy_witness": degeneracy_witness(n, u),
        "normal_form_automorphism": (u % n) if nd else None,
    }


def exhaustive_cross_check(n: int, u: int) -> bool:
    """O(n^4) brute-force confirmation of the O(log n) criterion."""
    e = pairing_exponent(n, u)
    els: List[Vec] = [(a, b) for a in range(n) for b in range(n)]
    brute = all(
        any(e(v, w) != 0 for w in els)
        for v in els if v != (0, 0)
    )
    return brute == is_nondegenerate(n, u)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for n in (5, 6, 12):
        for u in range(n):
            cert = certify(n, u)
            assert exhaustive_cross_check(n, u)
            print(cert)

algorithms.name: Aggregate Signature Construction and Single-Equation Pairing Verification
algorithms.description: Implements the signature scheme and its aggregation in the asymmetric setting: public key pk = sk·g₂, hashed message H = h·g₁, signature σ = sk·H, and verification e(σ,g₂) = e(H,pk). Aggregation of m signatures is the plain group sum, costing m−1 group additions and producing a single group element regardless of m; the aggregate is then checked by the one equation e(σ,g₂) = ∏ᵢ e(Hᵢ,pkᵢ), costing m+1 pairing evaluations and m−1 multiplications in the target group. Correctness is bilinearity: both sides equal ζ^(Σᵢ skᵢhᵢ). The module also implements weighted batch verification, e(Σᵢ rᵢσᵢ, g₂) = ∏ᵢ e(Hᵢ,pkᵢ)^{rᵢ}, which passes for every weight vector exactly when every individual signature is valid — taking indicator weights recovers any single check, which is the deterministic core of randomised batch verification. Signature size is O(1) in m; verification work is O(m) pairings, all of which may be precomputed on the key side since the public keys are known in advance.
algorithms.pseudocode:
SETUP: generators g₁ (signature group), g₂ (key group), root ζ = e(g₁,g₂) of exact order n

1. KEY GENERATION
   choose sk ∈ {0,…,n−1};  pk ← sk · g₂

2. SIGNING (one scalar multiplication, no randomness)
   H ← HashToGroup(message)          ▷ H = h · g₁
   σ ← sk · H

3. SINGLE VERIFICATION
   accept  ⟺  e(σ, g₂) = e(H, pk)

4. AGGREGATION                                    ▷ m−1 group additions, output size O(1)
   σ_agg ← 0
   for i = 1 … m:  σ_agg ← σ_agg + σᵢ

5. AGGREGATE VERIFICATION                          ▷ m+1 pairings
   R ← 1
   for i = 1 … m:  R ← R · e(Hᵢ, pkᵢ)
   accept  ⟺  e(σ_agg, g₂) = R

6. WEIGHTED BATCH VERIFICATION
   L ← e( Σᵢ rᵢ·σᵢ , g₂ )
   R ← ∏ᵢ e(Hᵢ, pkᵢ)^{rᵢ}
   accept  ⟺  L = R
   ▷ holding for all weight vectors r ⟺ every individual signature verifies
     (take rⱼ = [j = i₀] to isolate signer i₀)
algorithms.code:
"""
Algorithm 2: Aggregate Signature Construction and Single-Equation
Pairing Verification.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

Vec = Tuple[int, int]


def add(n: int, v: Vec, w: Vec) -> Vec:
    return ((v[0] + w[0]) % n, (v[1] + w[1]) % n)


def smul(n: int, k: int, v: Vec) -> Vec:
    return ((k * v[0]) % n, (k * v[1]) % n)


def pair(n: int, v: Vec, w: Vec) -> int:
    """Exponent of the pairing value: e(v,w) = zeta_0^(v1*w2 - v2*w1)."""
    return (v[0] * w[1] - v[1] * w[0]) % n


G1: Vec = (1, 0)  # signature generator
G2: Vec = (0, 1)  # key generator


def public_key(n: int, sk: int) -> Vec:
    """pk = sk * g2."""
    return smul(n, sk, G2)


def hash_point(n: int, h: int) -> Vec:
    """H = h * g1, the image of a message under hash-to-curve."""
    return smul(n, h, G1)


def sign(n: int, sk: int, h: int) -> Vec:
    """sigma = sk * H = (sk*h) * g1.  One scalar multiplication, no nonce."""
    return smul(n, sk * h, G1)


def aggregate(n: int, sigmas: Sequence[Vec]) -> Vec:
    """
    The aggregate signature is the plain group sum of the individual
    signatures.  Cost: m - 1 group additions; output size is one group
    element, independent of m.
    """
    acc: Vec = (0, 0)
    for s in sigmas:
        acc = add(n, acc, s)
    return acc


def aggregate_verify(
    n: int, pks: Sequence[Vec], hashes: Sequence[Vec], sigma: Vec
) -> bool:
    """
    Check the single aggregate equation

        e(sigma, g2)  ==  prod_i e(H_i, pk_i).

    Cost: m + 1 pairing evaluations and m - 1 multiplications in the target
    group.  Correctness is bilinearity: both sides equal zeta^(sum_i sk_i h_i)
    for honest inputs.  (In the exponent representation used here, the product
    on the right is a sum modulo n.)
    """
    rhs = 0
    for pk, hp in zip(pks, hashes):
        rhs = (rhs + pair(n, hp, pk)) % n
    return pair(n, sigma, G2) == rhs


def batch_verify(
    n: int,
    pks: Sequence[Vec],
    hashes: Sequence[Vec],
    sigmas: Sequence[Vec],
    weights: Sequence[int],
) -> bool:
    """
    Weighted batch verification:

        e( sum_i r_i sigma_i , g2 )  ==  prod_i e(H_i, pk_i)^{r_i}.

    Passing this for every weight vector is equivalent to every individual
    signature verifying; taking indicator weights recovers a single check.
    """
    lhs_pt: Vec = (0, 0)
    for r, s in zip(weights, sigmas):
        lhs_pt = add(n, lhs_pt, smul(n, r, s))
    rhs = 0
    for r, pk, hp in zip(weights, pks, hashes):
        rhs = (rhs + r * pair(n, hp, pk)) % n
    return pair(n, lhs_pt, G2) == rhs


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 11
    sks: List[int] = [3, 5, 8, 2]
    hs: List[int] = [4, 9, 1, 7]
    pks = [public_key(n, sk) for sk in sks]
    hashes = [hash_point(n, h) for h in hs]
    sigs = [sign(n, sk, h) for sk, h in zip(sks, hs)]
    agg = aggregate(n, sigs)
    print("individual signatures:", sigs)
    print("aggregate            :", agg)
    print("aggregate verifies   :", aggregate_verify(n, pks, hashes, agg))
    print("batch (weights 1..4) :", batch_verify(n, pks, hashes, sigs, [1, 2, 3, 4]))

algorithms.name: Aggregate-to-Single Forgery Extraction and the Diffie–Hellman Reduction
algorithms.description: The security reduction, made executable. Given any group element σ that satisfies the aggregate verification equation for a signer set containing the target index i₀ — with no assumption whatsoever about how σ was produced — the algorithm subtracts the contributions skᵢ·Hᵢ of every co-signer whose secret key is known, and returns the residual. The residual is provably a valid single-signer signature for i₀, because subtraction in the first argument of the pairing divides in the target group, and dividing the aggregate equation by the co-signers' factors leaves exactly e(H_{i₀}, pk_{i₀}). Cost is O(m) group operations with no rewinding and no oracle access. Composed with random-oracle programming — the signer's key set to the challenge a·g₂ and the fresh target message hashed to h·g₁ — signature uniqueness upgrades this to an equality rather than a mere implication: the extracted element equals the computational Diffie–Hellman target a·(h·g₁) exactly, making the reduction tight with no security loss. The routine verifies both the validity and the identification with the Diffie–Hellman target. Note the load-bearing hypothesis: the co-signers' secret keys must be known, i.e. keys must be registered.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: aggregate σ accepted for signer set S; target index i₀ ∈ S;
       co-signer secret keys {skᵢ : i ∈ S, i ≠ i₀};  hash exponents {hᵢ}
OUTPUT: a valid single-signer signature for i₀ — equal to the CDH target under programming

1. PRECONDITION CHECK
   assert  e(σ, g₂) = ∏_{i∈S} e(Hᵢ, pkᵢ)

2. STRIP THE KNOWN CO-SIGNERS                      ▷ O(m) group operations
   σ′ ← σ
   for each i ∈ S with i ≠ i₀:
       σ′ ← σ′ − skᵢ · Hᵢ

3. VALIDITY (theorem, verified here)
   e(σ′, g₂) = e(σ, g₂) · ∏_{i≠i₀} e(Hᵢ, pkᵢ)^{−1} = e(H_{i₀}, pk_{i₀})
   so σ′ is accepted as a single-signer signature for i₀

4. REDUCTION TO COMPUTATIONAL DIFFIE–HELLMAN
   given challenge (a·g₂, h·g₁):
       program pk_{i₀} ← a·g₂  and  H_{i₀} ← h·g₁  for a FRESH target message
       by uniqueness of signatures,  σ′ = (a·h)·g₁ = a·(h·g₁) = CDH answer
   ▷ the forgery IS the solution: no factor stripped, no rewinding, no loss

5. return σ′

algorithms.name: Rogue-Key Universal Forgery against Unregistered Aggregation
algorithms.description: The attack that proves the registered-key hypothesis of the extraction reduction is indispensable. Reading only the victim's public key pk₁ — no secret key, no interaction, no signing queries — the adversary picks an arbitrary scalar y and publishes the rogue public key pk₂ = y·g₂ − pk₁, then outputs σ = y·H as a two-signer aggregate on a common message H. Verification succeeds because e(H,pk₁)·e(H,pk₂) = e(H, pk₁ + (y·g₂ − pk₁)) = e(H,y·g₂) = e(y·H,g₂), an unconditional identity: the victim's key cancels algebraically. The attack costs two group operations and one scalar multiplication, and its success probability is exactly 1 — there is no failure case and nothing to tune. The module includes an exhaustive sweep over every adversarial scalar, victim key and message in a small model, confirming a success rate of 1.0. The defence is to require a proof of possession of the secret key at registration, or to use a defended aggregation rule in which each public key is exponentiated by a hash of the entire key set, destroying the cancellation.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: victim public key pk₁ (public information only); a common message with hash point H
OUTPUT: a two-signer aggregate that verifies, implicating the victim

1. CHOOSE AN ARBITRARY SCALAR
   pick y ∈ {0,…,n−1}                     ▷ any value works; no secrecy needed

2. FORGE THE PUBLIC KEY                    ▷ 1 scalar multiplication + 1 subtraction
   pk₂ ← y·g₂ − pk₁
   ▷ computed from pk₁ alone; the adversary knows no matching secret key

3. FORGE THE AGGREGATE SIGNATURE           ▷ 1 scalar multiplication
   σ ← y·H

4. THE VERIFIER ACCEPTS, UNCONDITIONALLY
   e(H,pk₁)·e(H,pk₂) = e(H, pk₁ + y·g₂ − pk₁) = e(H, y·g₂) = e(H,g₂)^y = e(y·H, g₂) = e(σ,g₂)

5. AUDIT
   for every y, every victim key pk₁ and every message H in a small model:
       assert the forged aggregate verifies       ▷ measured success rate: 1.0

DEFENCE: demand a proof of possession at key registration, or aggregate with each key
         exponentiated by a hash of the full key set, which blocks the cancellation.

visualizations.name: The Pairing Table and the Symplectic Blind Spot
visualizations.description: Two panels rendering the algebraic core. The left panel is the full 25×25 table of pairing exponents det(v,w) on (Z/5)², in which alternation appears as a zero diagonal and skew-symmetry as antisymmetry about it — a direct picture of the two axioms. The right panel restricts the same pairing to a single cyclic subgroup ⟨v₀⟩ and finds it identically zero, annotated cell by cell. That vanishing is the rank obstruction: an alternating pairing is blind inside any one direction of the torsion, so nondegeneracy in rank one would force the group to be trivial, and pairing-based cryptography must be two-dimensional.
visualizations.code:
"""
Visualization 1: The pairing table of the determinant form, and the
symplectic blind spot.

Left panel:  the full N x N table of exponents  det(v, w)  on (Z/n)^2,
             N = n^2.  The table is antisymmetric with a zero diagonal --
             a picture of alternation and skew-symmetry.
Right panel: the same table restricted to a single cyclic subgroup <v0>,
             which is identically zero.  This is the rank obstruction:
             an alternating pairing sees nothing inside one "line" of the
             torsion group, so nondegeneracy is impossible in rank one.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

Vec = Tuple[int, int]


def elements(n: int) -> List[Vec]:
    return [(a, b) for a in range(n) for b in range(n)]


def det_form(n: int, v: Vec, w: Vec) -> int:
    return (v[0] * w[1] - v[1] * w[0]) % n


def pairing_table(n: int) -> np.ndarray:
    els = elements(n)
    return np.array([[det_form(n, v, w) for w in els] for v in els])


def cyclic_table(n: int, v0: Vec) -> np.ndarray:
    pts = [((a * v0[0]) % n, (a * v0[1]) % n) for a in range(n)]
    return np.array([[det_form(n, v, w) for w in pts] for v in pts])


def main() -> None:
    n = 5
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.6))

    tab = pairing_table(n)
    im0 = axes[0].imshow(tab, cmap="twilight", interpolation="nearest")
    axes[0].set_title(
        f"Pairing exponents  det(v,w)  on  (Z/{n})²\n"
        "zero diagonal = alternation;  antisymmetric = skew-symmetry",
        fontsize=11,
    )
    axes[0].set_xlabel("w  (indexed over all 25 group elements)")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("v")
    fig.colorbar(im0, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.046, label="exponent of ζ")

    v0 = (1, 2)
    ctab = cyclic_table(n, v0)
    im1 = axes[1].imshow(
        ctab, cmap="twilight", interpolation="nearest", vmin=0, vmax=n - 1
    )
    axes[1].set_title(
        f"Restriction to the cyclic subgroup ⟨{v0}⟩\n"
        "identically zero: the pairing is blind on a line",
        fontsize=11,
    )
    axes[1].set_xlabel("b   (w = b·v₀)")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("a   (v = a·v₀)")
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            axes[1].text(j, i, str(ctab[i, j]), ha="center", va="center",
                         color="white", fontsize=11)
    fig.colorbar(im1, ax=axes[1], fraction=0.046, label="exponent of ζ")

    fig.suptitle(
        "Alternation forces the determinant — and forbids rank one",
        fontsize=13, fontweight="bold",
    )
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("pairing_tables.png", dpi=150)
    print("wrote pairing_tables.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: Exact Aggregate Compression: N^m Tuples onto N Aggregates
visualizations.description: A measurement of the compression theorem. The left panel plots, on a logarithmic scale, the number of m-tuples of signatures (N^m, growing exponentially in the number of signers) against the measured number of distinct aggregates, which stays pinned at exactly N for every m ≥ 1 — the aggregation map is onto the whole group, so the compression is exactly N^m ↠ N and not into some thinner, structured subset. The right panel restates the same fact in deployment units: total signature bandwidth for m signers at a 255-bit group, with and without aggregation, showing the entire m-dependence migrating out of the signature and into the public keys, which are known in advance anyway.
visualizations.code:
"""
Visualization 2: Exact aggregate compression,  N^m  signature tuples
collapsing onto  N  aggregates.

Left panel:  the number of distinct m-tuples of signatures, N^m, against the
             number of distinct aggregates, which is exactly N for every
             m >= 1 -- the aggregation map is onto the whole group.
Right panel: the same statement in the units that matter in practice: total
             signature bandwidth for m signers, with and without aggregation,
             at a 255-bit group.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Vec = Tuple[int, int]


def aggregation_image_size(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Number of distinct values of (s_1,...,s_m) |-> s_1 + ... + s_m."""
    els: List[Vec] = [(a, b) for a in range(n) for b in range(n)]
    image = set()
    for tup in product(els, repeat=m):
        acc = (0, 0)
        for v in tup:
            acc = ((acc[0] + v[0]) % n, (acc[1] + v[1]) % n)
        image.add(acc)
    return len(image)


def main() -> None:
    n = 3
    N = n * n
    ms = [1, 2, 3, 4]
    tuples = [N ** m for m in ms]
    images = [aggregation_image_size(n, m) for m in ms]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.2))

    axes[0].semilogy(ms, tuples, "o-", lw=2, label=f"tuples of signatures: $N^m$ (N={N})")
    axes[0].semilogy(ms, images, "s-", lw=2, label="distinct aggregates (measured)")
    axes[0].axhline(N, ls="--", c="grey", lw=1)
    axes[0].set_xticks(ms)
    axes[0].set_xlabel("number of signers  m")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("count (log scale)")
    axes[0].set_title(
        f"Exact compression over (Z/{n})²:  $N^m \\twoheadrightarrow N$\n"
        "the image is the entire group, no thinner",
        fontsize=11,
    )
    axes[0].legend()
    axes[0].grid(alpha=0.3)

    big_ms = [1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000]
    bits_plain = [255 * m for m in big_ms]
    bits_agg = [255 for _ in big_ms]
    axes[1].loglog(big_ms, bits_plain, "o-", lw=2, label="separate signatures")
    axes[1].loglog(big_ms, bits_agg, "s-", lw=2, label="one aggregate")
    axes[1].set_xlabel("number of signers  m")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("signature bandwidth (bits)")
    axes[1].set_title(
        "Bandwidth at a 255-bit group\n"
        "the m-dependence migrates entirely into the public keys",
        fontsize=11,
    )
    axes[1].legend()
    axes[1].grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")

    fig.suptitle("How short is short? The compression theorem, measured",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("compression.png", dpi=150)
    print("wrote compression.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: The Classification of Alternating Pairings, Counted
visualizations.description: Every alternating pairing on (Z/n)² is ζ^(u·det) for a single scalar u, and the classification theorem says it is nondegenerate exactly when u is a unit. The left panel draws the grid of pairs (n,u) coloured by the exact order of the root of unity as a fraction of n, with the units marked: the full-order cells and the marked cells coincide, and every unmarked cell carries an explicit degeneracy witness (n/gcd(u,n), 0). The right panel counts the nondegenerate pairings for each modulus up to 40 and overlays Euler's totient φ(n); the two agree exactly, so there are precisely n−1 nondegenerate alternating pairings when n is prime, and all of them are primitive powers of the determinant form.
visualizations.code:
"""
Visualization 3: The classification of alternating pairings -- which scalars
give a nondegenerate pairing, and how the root of unity loses order.

Every alternating pairing on (Z/n)^2 valued in mu_n is  e_u(v,w) = zeta^{u det(v,w)}
for a single scalar u in Z/n.  It is nondegenerate exactly when u is a unit,
in which case its root of unity has full order n; otherwise the root's order
drops to n / gcd(u, n) and an explicit degeneracy witness (n/gcd, 0) exists.

Left panel:  the grid (n, u), coloured by the exact order of the root of unity,
             with units marked.  The units form the nondegenerate locus.
Right panel: the count of nondegenerate pairings against Euler's totient
             phi(n) -- they coincide exactly.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def root_order(n: int, u: int) -> int:
    return n // gcd(u % n, n)


def euler_phi(n: int) -> int:
    return sum(1 for a in range(n) if gcd(a, n) == 1)


def count_nondegenerate(n: int) -> int:
    return sum(1 for u in range(n) if gcd(u, n) == 1)


def main() -> None:
    n_max = 16
    grid = np.full((n_max, n_max), np.nan)
    for n in range(1, n_max + 1):
        for u in range(n):
            grid[n - 1, u] = root_order(n, u) / n

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.5, 5.6))

    im = axes[0].imshow(grid, cmap="viridis", origin="lower",
                        extent=(-0.5, n_max - 0.5, 0.5, n_max + 0.5),
                        aspect="auto", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    for n in range(1, n_max + 1):
        for u in range(n):
            if gcd(u, n) == 1:
                axes[0].plot(u, n, marker="o", ms=3.2, color="white")
    axes[0].set_xlabel("scalar  u  (the pairing is  ζ^{u·det})")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("modulus  n")
    axes[0].set_title(
        "Order of the root of unity, as a fraction of n\n"
        "white dots = units = exactly the nondegenerate pairings",
        fontsize=11,
    )
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.046, label="ord(ζ) / n")

    ns: List[int] = list(range(1, 41))
    counts = [count_nondegenerate(n) for n in ns]
    phis = [euler_phi(n) for n in ns]
    axes[1].plot(ns, counts, "o", ms=6, label="nondegenerate alternating pairings")
    axes[1].plot(ns, phis, "-", lw=1.5, label=r"Euler totient $\varphi(n)$")
    axes[1].set_xlabel("modulus  n")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("count")
    axes[1].set_title(
        "The classification, counted\n"
        r"nondegenerate pairings $\leftrightarrow (\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$,"
        " so there are exactly n−1 for n prime",
        fontsize=11,
    )
    axes[1].legend()
    axes[1].grid(alpha=0.3)

    fig.suptitle("There is essentially one Weil pairing, up to a unit",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("classification.png", dpi=150)
    print("wrote classification.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.title: The Pairing Laboratory: From One Axiom to Short Signatures and Back to a Total Break
interactive_demos.description: A single six-tab exploratory environment in which every result of the development can be manipulated and recomputed live inside the determinant model (Z/n)². Tab 1 evaluates the pairing on user-chosen vectors and certifies alternation, skew-symmetry, bilinearity and blindness on cyclic subgroups simultaneously — set w to a multiple of v and watch the exponent collapse to zero, which is the rank obstruction in miniature. Tab 2 sweeps the classification scalar u against the modulus n, displaying the pairing table with the degeneracy witness row highlighted the moment u shares a factor with n, and reporting the count of nondegenerate pairings as φ(n). Tab 3 mounts the decisional Diffie–Hellman distinguisher using only the public group elements aP, bQ, cQ, showing the publicly computable test agreeing exactly with the hidden relation c ≡ ab, alongside the MOV table witnessing injectivity of a ↦ e(aP,Q). Tab 4 runs the signature scheme and tests every candidate signature in the group at once, lighting up exactly one — signature uniqueness made visible — and shows that the accepted signature is literally the Diffie–Hellman target, which is what makes the security reduction tight. Tab 5 aggregates three signers into one group element, verifies the single aggregate equation, and executes the aggregate-to-single forgery extraction live. Tab 6 mounts the rogue-key attack: with no secret key and no interaction, the adversary's forged two-signer aggregate is accepted for every setting of every slider, demonstrating that the registered-key hypothesis of the reduction cannot be dropped. Progressive-disclosure panels throughout carry the proofs, including the two-line derivation of the determinant form and the obstruction theorem showing that the naive symmetric model is satisfiable only for trivial torsion.
interactive_demos.html:
The Pairing Laboratory Alternation forces a determinant — and the determinant runs the whole show: classification, the rank obstruction, the collapse of decisional Diffie–Hellman, unique signatures, aggregation, and the rogue-key attack. Everything below is computed live.

1 · The pairing itself
2 · Classification
3 · DDH collapses
4 · Signing & uniqueness
5 · Aggregation
6 · Rogue-key attack

The group is (Z/n)². The pairing sends a pair of elements to an n-th root of unity ζk; we display the exponent k. Move the sliders and watch three theorems hold simultaneously: the diagonal is always 0 (alternation), swapping the arguments negates the exponent (skew-symmetry), and the exponent is always the determinant v₁w₂ − v₂w₁.

e(v,w)
e(w,v)
e(v,v)
e(2v,3w)
Why must the exponent be a determinant? (click for the two-line proof)

Write v = a·e₁ + b·e₂ and w = c·e₁ + d·e₂ and expand by additivity in each slot. You get four terms. The terms e(a e₁, c e₁) and e(b e₂, d e₂) are 1, because e(x,x)=1 makes the pairing blind on any single line. The remaining two are e(e₁,e₂)ad and e(e₂,e₁)bc = e(e₁,e₂)−bc, using skew-symmetry — which is itself a consequence of alternation, obtained by expanding 1 = e(v+w, v+w). Multiplying gives ζad−bc. Nobody put a determinant in the axioms; it came out.

The rank obstruction: why cryptography needs two directions

Set w to a multiple of v above — say w = 2v — and the exponent collapses to 0, always. An alternating pairing is identically trivial on any cyclic subgroup. So if the whole torsion group were cyclic, nondegeneracy would force it to be zero. A nontrivial nondegenerate pairing can only live on rank-two torsion — which is exactly why pairing-based schemes use two generators.

Every alternating pairing on (Z/n)² is eu(v,w) = ζu·det(v,w) for a single scalar u. The classification theorem says eu is nondegenerate — no nonzero vector pairs trivially with everything — precisely when u is invertible modulo n. When it is not, the vector (n/gcd(u,n), 0) is an explicit blind spot.

gcd(u,n)
order of ζu
Symplectic normal form — there is essentially only one pairing

If u is a unit, let ψ be multiplication by u, an automorphism of the group. Then eu(v,w) = det(ψv, w): every nondegenerate alternating pairing is the determinant pairing composed with a change of basis. Consequently the number of nondegenerate alternating pairings is exactly φ(n), and n−1 when n is prime. Practically: to identify any construction with the Weil pairing, you only need to compute its value on one basis pair — the rest is forced.

Here is the gift and the curse. Given only the group elements aP, bQ, cQ — never the secret exponents — anyone can compute the test e(aP,bQ) =? e(P,cQ). It succeeds exactly when c ≡ ab. So the decisional Diffie–Hellman problem is easy in a pairing group, and no security proof may rest on it. The computational problem — actually producing abP — is what survives, and it is what the signature scheme is reduced to.

MOV embedding: the map a ↦ e(aP,Q) = ζa
The attacker also needs two directions

Take all three inputs from a single cyclic subgroup — replace Q by P. Then both sides of the test are 1 by blindness, and the test says nothing at all. The same rank-two requirement that makes the protocol possible makes the attack possible; neither exists in rank one.

The scheme. Secret key sk, public key pk = sk·g₂, message hashed to H = h·g₁, signature σ = sk·H, verification e(σ, g₂) = e(H, pk). Below, every candidate signature s·g₁ in the signature group is tested. Exactly one is accepted — the honest one. That is signature uniqueness, and it is what makes the security reduction perfectly tight.

public key
hash point H
signature σ
CDH target
All candidate signatures s·g₁ — green = accepted
Why a forgery is the Diffie–Hellman answer

Program the hash oracle so that the target message — one the adversary never asked the signer to sign — hashes to the challenge point h·g₁, and set the signer's public key to the challenge a·g₂. If the adversary outputs anything the verifier accepts, uniqueness says it equals (a·h)·g₁ = a·(h·g₁), which is precisely the Diffie–Hellman answer. No factor to strip, no rewinding: the forgery is the solution. Compare the "CDH target" card above with the signature — they are the same element.

The trap: why a symmetric setup with injective verification cannot exist

It is tempting to use one generator G and simply demand that P ↦ e(P,G) be injective, since that would give uniqueness for free. But alternation gives e(G,G) = 1 = e(0,G), so injectivity forces G = 0; and then e(Q,G) = 1 for every Q, forcing Q = 0 too. Such a model exists only when the whole torsion group is trivial, and every theorem proved in it is vacuously true. The asymmetric setup used here — two generators and the requirement that ζ = e(g₁,g₂) have exact order n — is satisfiable and delivers the same uniqueness as a theorem instead of an axiom.

Add the signatures together. One group element now certifies all of them, through the single equation e(σ, g₂) = ∏ᵢ e(Hᵢ, pkᵢ). Change any signer's key or message and the aggregate changes; the equation tracks it exactly. The panel also runs the security reduction: strip the co-signers' known contributions from the aggregate and what remains is a valid single-signer signature — in fact the Diffie–Hellman answer for signer 1.

3 signatures cost
aggregate costs
The compression theorem, exactly

If the group has N elements, the space of m-tuples of signatures has Nm elements, while an aggregate is a single group element. More than that: every group element occurs as an aggregate (put the value you want in the first slot and zeros elsewhere), so the image is the whole group — the compression is exactly Nm ↠ N, no thinner. Nothing is hidden in a sparse subset that an attacker could exploit; the entire m-dependence has moved into the public keys, which are known in advance anyway.

Now break it. Suppose signers may publish any public key they like, with no proof that they know the matching secret. The adversary reads the victim's public key pk₁, picks any scalar y, and publishes the rogue key pk₂ = y·g₂ − pk₁. Then σ = y·H — computed with no secret key and no interaction whatsoever — passes the two-signer aggregate check. Every time. Move any slider you like; the verdict never changes.

victim pk₁
rogue pk₂
forged σ = y·H
secrets used
none
Why the security proof needs registered keys

The reduction from aggregate forgery to single-signer forgery works by subtracting the co-signers' contributions skᵢ·Hᵢ from the aggregate — which the reduction can only do if it knows those secret keys. The rogue-key attack is the exact demonstration that this hypothesis is load-bearing: without registration the attacker chooses a key that algebraically cancels the victim's, and the cancellation is unconditional. Deployments therefore require a proof of possession at registration, or use a defended aggregation rule in which each key is exponentiated by a hash of the whole key set, which destroys the cancellation.

interactive_layout:
# The Determinant Hidden Inside Elliptic Curves ### A guided tour of alternating pairings, short signatures, and the one axiom that decides everything --- ## Where we are going There is a digital signature scheme in which a thousand people, who have never met, can each sign a different message, and all thousand signatures can then be added together into a single object no larger than one signature — with one equation still certifying that all thousand really signed. The engine is the **Weil pairing** on an elliptic curve. This page builds that machine from scratch. The remarkable thing is how little we have to assume. One axiom, imposed on an otherwise ordinary bilinear map, forces a $2\times2$ determinant to appear; and from that determinant follow the classification of all pairings, the reason cryptography needs two independent directions in the torsion, the reason decisional Diffie–Hellman is *easy* in a pairing group, the uniqueness and shortness of signatures, and — if one is careless — a total break of the scheme. Everything on this page is live. Nothing is a static picture of a special case: move a slider and the mathematics recomputes. --- ## 1. Bilinearity, and one extra axiom Let $A$ be an abelian group written additively — think of the points on an elliptic curve killed by multiplication by $n$, the **$n$-torsion**. A **pairing** is a map $e : A \times A \to \mu$ into a commutative group $\mu$ (concretely, the $n$-th roots of unity), additive in each slot: $$e(P + P', Q) = e(P,Q)\,e(P',Q), \qquad e(P, Q+Q') = e(P,Q)\,e(P,Q').$$ Bilinearity alone already gives the identity that makes pairings useful: $$e(aP,\, bQ) = e(P,Q)^{ab}.$$ A verifier who can compute $e$ can *check a product of secret exponents without learning them*. Hold that thought — it is the whole of pairing-based cryptography in one line. Now add the axiom that makes a pairing a *Weil* pairing: $$e(P,P) = 1 \quad\text{for every } P.$$ This is **alternation**. It looks innocuous. It is not.
Three immediate consequences (click to unfold) **Skew-symmetry.** Expand $1 = e(P+Q,P+Q)$ by bilinearity. The diagonal terms die by alternation, leaving $e(P,Q)e(Q,P)=1$, i.e. $e(Q,P) = e(P,Q)^{-1}$. Antisymmetry was never assumed; it is a theorem. (Over groups of even order the two conditions genuinely differ, and alternation is the stronger one.) **Blindness on a line.** If $P = aR$ and $Q = bR$ are multiples of a common point, then $e(aR,bR) = e(R,R)^{ab} = 1$. An alternating pairing is *identically trivial* on any cyclic subgroup — it sees nothing inside a single direction of the torsion. **The determinant.** Let $A$ be generated by $e_1, e_2$ and put $\zeta = e(e_1,e_2)$. Expanding $e(ae_1+be_2,\;ce_1+de_2)$ gives four terms; the two diagonal ones vanish by alternation; the two cross terms combine by skew-symmetry, and out drops $$e(ae_1+be_2,\ ce_1+de_2) = \zeta^{\,ad-bc}.$$ The exponent is the **determinant**. Nobody put it into the axioms.
Try it. The widget below computes the pairing in the model group $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^2$, displaying the exponent of $\zeta$. Watch the diagonal stay at $0$, watch swapping the arguments negate the exponent, and set $w$ to a multiple of $v$ to watch the pairing go blind. {{interactive_demo:0}} > **Try this first.** In tab 1, set $v = (1,2)$ and $w = (2,4)$ — a multiple of $v$. The exponent collapses to > $0$. Then nudge $w_2$ by one and it springs back to life. That collapse is the single most consequential > fact on this page. --- ## 2. What the collapse costs: rank one is impossible Here is the theorem that the collapse implies. > **Rank obstruction.** *If the $n$-torsion is cyclic — generated by one point $g$ — and carries a > nondegenerate alternating pairing, then the $n$-torsion is trivial.*
Proof (two lines) Every element is a multiple of $g$, so by blindness $e(g,Q) = 1$ for all $Q$. Nondegeneracy — no nonzero element pairs trivially with everything — forces $g = 0$. Since everything is a multiple of $g$, everything is $0$. $\blacksquare$
Contrapositively: **a nontrivial nondegenerate Weil pairing can only live on rank-two torsion.** For elliptic curves this matches the classical structure theorem $E[n]\cong(\mathbb{Z}/n)^2$ when $n$ is prime to the characteristic — but note that we did not use the structure theorem to prove it. The obstruction is pure pairing algebra, and it explains *why* rank two is needed at all. Symmetric ("type-1") pairing setups require a distortion map for exactly this reason. The picture below shows both halves at once: the full antisymmetric pairing table on $(\mathbb{Z}/5)^2$, and the same table restricted to a single cyclic subgroup, where it is identically zero. {{visualization:0}} --- ## 3. How many pairings are there? Exactly $\varphi(n)$ Once the determinant is forced, the only remaining freedom is a single scalar. > **Classification.** *Every alternating pairing on $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^2$ valued in $\mu_n$ has the form > $e_u(v,w) = \zeta^{\,u\det(v,w)}$ with $\det(v,w) = v_1w_2 - v_2w_1$, for a single $u \in \mathbb{Z}/n$ > determined by the value on the standard basis.* > > **Nondegeneracy criterion.** *$e_u$ is nondegenerate if and only if $u$ is a unit modulo $n$. Hence the > nondegenerate alternating pairings correspond bijectively to $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$: there are > $\varphi(n)$ of them, and exactly $n-1$ when $n$ is prime.* > > **Symplectic normal form.** *Every nondegenerate alternating pairing is the determinant pairing composed > with an automorphism: $e(v,w) = \det(\psi v, w)$. The Weil pairing is unique up to a change of basis.*
Why degeneracy has an explicit witness Suppose $u$ is not a unit, so $g = \gcd(u,n) > 1$. Put $k = n/g$, so $0 < k < n$ and $ku \equiv 0$. Then $v = (k,0)$ is nonzero, yet $u\det(v,w) = u\,k\,w_2 = 0$ for every $w$. So $v$ pairs trivially with the entire group: an explicit blind spot. Conversely, if $u$ is a unit, testing against $\varepsilon_2$ kills $v_1$ and testing against $\varepsilon_1$ kills $v_2$, so only $v = 0$ is blind.
Tab 2 of the laboratory lets you sweep $u$ and $n$ and watch a whole row of the pairing table go to zero the moment $u$ shares a factor with $n$. The certificate below does the same thing algorithmically, in $O(\log n)$ instead of the naive $O(n^4)$, and cross-checks itself against brute force. {{algorithm:0}} And here is the classification in aggregate: which scalars are nondegenerate, how the order of the root of unity degrades, and the exact agreement of the count with Euler's totient. {{visualization:2}} --- ## 4. The pairing is a gift to the attacker too Three classical consequences, all one-liners in this framework. **Degree law.** $e(mP, mQ) = e(P,Q)^{m^2}$. More generally an endomorphism with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ scales the pairing by $ad-bc$. Multiplication by $m$ has determinant $m^2$, which is the degree of the multiplication-by-$m$ isogeny: the algebraic shadow of a geometric fact. **MOV embedding.** If $\zeta = e(P,Q)$ has exact order $n$, then $a \mapsto e(aP,Q) = \zeta^a$ is injective on $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$. An attacker facing "find $a$ from $aP$" on the curve can pair with $Q$ and instead solve a discrete logarithm in a finite field, where index calculus is far more powerful. This is why pairing-friendly curves must have a carefully chosen embedding degree — large enough that the finite-field problem stays hard. **Decisional Diffie–Hellman collapses.** Given only the group elements $aP$, $bQ$, $cQ$ — never the exponents — anyone can compute $$e(aP,bQ) \;\overset{?}{=}\; e(P,cQ),$$ and the test holds precisely when $c \equiv ab \pmod n$. So DDH is *easy* here, and no security proof in a pairing group may rest on it. What survives is the **computational** problem: given $a\,g_2$ and $h\,g_1$, actually produce $ah\,g_1$. Go to tab 3 and set the "claim" $c$ to the true product — the public test flips to agreement. Set it anywhere else and it flips back. The attacker never sees $a$ or $b$. > **A pleasing coda.** Drop all three inputs into a single cyclic subgroup and the DDH test becomes vacuous: > both sides are $1$ by blindness. The attack, like the protocol, needs two independent directions. Rank two > is the price of admission for everyone. --- ## 5. Signing with a pairing — and a trap The scheme is almost too simple. Fix a signature generator $g_1$ and a key generator $g_2$, and let $\zeta = e(g_1,g_2)$. | object | definition | |---|---| | secret key | a number $sk$ | | public key | $pk = sk\cdot g_2$ | | hashed message | $H = h\cdot g_1$ | | signature | $\sigma = sk\cdot H$ | | verification | $e(\sigma, g_2) \;=\; e(H, pk)$ | Correctness is bilinearity: both sides are $\zeta^{sk\,h}$. The signature is one group element — roughly 48 bytes at standard security levels — with no randomness and hence no nonce-reuse catastrophe. But there is a sharper statement than "the honest signature verifies": > **Exact verification criterion.** *A candidate $s\cdot g_1$ is accepted if and only if > $s \equiv sk\cdot h \pmod n$, where $n$ is the exact order of $\zeta$. Consequently every accepted signature > equals the honest one: BLS signatures are unique.* Tab 4 tests **every** candidate signature in the group and lights up exactly one.
⚠ The trap: the most natural setup is mathematically impossible It is tempting to work symmetrically: one generator $G$, and — since uniqueness is what we want — simply *demand* that $P \mapsto e(P,G)$ be injective. This looks like a clean, strong nondegeneracy. It is self-contradictory. Alternation gives $e(G,G) = 1 = e(0,G)$, so injectivity forces $G = 0$; and then $e(Q,G) = e(Q,0) = 1 = e(0,0)$ for every $Q$, so injectivity forces $Q = 0$ too. > **Obstruction theorem.** *A setup with an alternating pairing and injective $P\mapsto e(P,G)$ exists only > when the entire $n$-torsion is trivial.* Every theorem proved in such a model — correctness, uniqueness, unforgeability — is true, and about nothing. This is not a bug in a proof; it is a bug in a *definition*, and it is exactly the kind that survives informal review because each ingredient is individually standard. The repair is what practice already uses: the **asymmetric (type-3) setting**, with two generators and the satisfiable requirement $\operatorname{ord}\big(e(g_1,g_2)\big) = n$. Signatures live in $\langle g_1\rangle$, where the verification map *is* injective — as a theorem, not an axiom. And unlike the symmetric model, this one has models: the determinant group $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^2$ for every $n\ge1$, and any curve with $E[n]\cong(\mathbb{Z}/n)^2$.
--- ## 6. Why forgery is exactly as hard as Diffie–Hellman The reduction is a programming argument, and uniqueness makes it perfectly tight. We are handed a computational Diffie–Hellman challenge: $a\,g_2$ and $h\,g_1$; produce $ah\,g_1$. Run the adversary with the signer's public key set to the challenge $a\,g_2$, and program the hash oracle so the target message hashes to $h\,g_1$. That message is **fresh** — never queried to the signing oracle — so we never have to sign something we cannot compute. Now suppose the adversary outputs any accepted signature $\sigma$ on the target message. Uniqueness says $\sigma$ is not merely *related to* the Diffie–Hellman answer. It **is** the answer: $$\sigma = a\cdot(h\,g_1).$$ No factor to strip, no rewinding, no loss. > **Existential unforgeability.** *If the Diffie–Hellman target lies outside the adversary's reach, then no > reachable group element passes verification on the fresh message.* In tab 4, compare the "signature" card with the "CDH target" card. They are the same element — that identity *is* the security proof. --- ## 7. A thousand signatures, one group element Aggregation is just addition: $$\sigma = \sum_{i\in S}\sigma_i, \qquad\text{verified by}\qquad e(\sigma,g_2) = \prod_{i\in S} e(H_i, pk_i).$$ Both sides are $\zeta^{\sum_i sk_i h_i}$, so correctness is once again bilinearity. Tab 5 runs three signers live; change any key or message and watch the equation track it. {{interactive_demo:0}} *(The laboratory above is the same widget — jump to tab 5 for aggregation and tab 6 for the attack.)* Here is the reduction that makes aggregation safe: > **Aggregate-to-single extraction.** *If $\sigma$ satisfies the aggregate equation for a signer set containing > the target $i_0$, and the co-signers' secret keys are known, then* > $$\sigma - \sum_{i \neq i_0} sk_i H_i$$ > *is a valid single-signer signature for $i_0$ — with no assumption on how $\sigma$ was produced.*
Proof: one computation Subtracting in the first slot divides in the target group (skew-symmetry). The aggregate equation says $e(\sigma,g_2) = \zeta^{\,\sum_i sk_ih_i}$; the co-signer sum pairs to $\zeta^{\Sigma}$ with $\Sigma = \sum_{i\ne i_0}sk_ih_i$; dividing leaves $\zeta^{\,sk_{i_0}h_{i_0}} = e(H_{i_0}, pk_{i_0})$. $\blacksquare$
Chain this with the programming argument and an aggregate forgery on a fresh message *is*, verbatim, the Diffie–Hellman answer. Aggregate unforgeability reduces to computational Diffie–Hellman with no loss. The two algorithms below implement aggregation-plus-verification and the extraction reduction respectively. {{algorithm:1}} {{algorithm:2}} --- ## 8. Exactly how short is short? "The aggregate is one group element, so it's short" is true but incomplete: it does not rule out the aggregate landing in some thin, structured subset of the group — which would itself be an attack surface. The precise statement rules that out. > **Compression theorem.** *Let the group have $N$ elements and let $m \geq 1$. The space of $m$-tuples of > signatures has $N^m$ elements; the set of values taken by aggregation has exactly $N$ elements. Aggregation > is precisely an $N^m \twoheadrightarrow N$ compression.* The surjectivity is easy — put the value you want in the first slot and zeros elsewhere — and it is the half that matters. Nothing is hidden; the entire $m$-dependence has migrated into the public keys, which are known in advance anyway. {{visualization:1}} At $N \approx 2^{255}$ and $m = 1000$, that is a $255{,}000$-bit object replaced by a $255$-bit one. > **Related practical point.** You can also *batch-verify* without aggregating: pick weights $r_i$ and check > $e(\sum_i r_i\sigma_i,\ g_2) = \prod_i e(H_i,pk_i)^{r_i}$. This passes for *all* weight vectors precisely > when every individual signature is valid — take the indicator weights to recover any single check. That > equivalence is the deterministic core of the randomised batch tricks used in production. --- ## 9. Now break it: the rogue-key attack The extraction theorem assumed the reduction knows the co-signers' keys. Is that hypothesis real, or an artefact of the proof? It is real, and the demonstration is brutal. Let $pk_1$ be an honest victim's public key. The adversary picks any $y$, computes the **rogue key** $$pk_2 = y\,g_2 - pk_1,$$ using nothing but the victim's *public* key, and publishes the "aggregate signature" $\sigma = y\cdot H$ on a common message. Check it: $$e(H,pk_1)\,e(H,pk_2) \;=\; e\big(H,\ pk_1 + (y g_2 - pk_1)\big) \;=\; e(H,\ y g_2) \;=\; e(yH,\ g_2).$$ Verification passes. The adversary knows no secret key, never contacted the victim, and has just produced a two-signer aggregate implicating them. The victim's key was *cancelled algebraically*. Tab 6 of the laboratory mounts the attack live. Move every slider you have; the verdict never changes, because the identity is unconditional. The algorithm below confirms a success rate of exactly $1$ over the entire parameter space. {{algorithm:3}} > **The remedy.** Require a proof of possession of the secret key at registration (the KOSK model), or use a > defended aggregation rule in which each public key is exponentiated by a hash of the whole key set — which > destroys the cancellation. This is not a theoretical nicety; it is why deployed aggregate-signature systems > demand key registration. --- ## 10.
